title: Sikandar and the Broken Temples
subtitle: In the Valleys of Faith and Fire
era: Reign of Sikandar But-Shikan, c. 1389-1413 CE
region: Srinagar, Martand, Parihaspore, Bijbehara and Anantnag
moral: Truth must be spoken without hatred and without hiding.

sources.note: Names Martand, Vijayesvara, Cakradhara, Suresvari, Varaha and Tripuresvara among destroyed shrines.
Adds temple names and reports forced conversions and massacres, while writing later and with its own pious framing.

sources.citation: Walter Slaje's studies; Chitralekha Zutshi, Languages of Belonging; Mohibbul Hasan, Kashmir Under the Sultans
sources.note: Modern debate over religious motive, realpolitik, Brahmin wealth and source bias.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Sikandar standing between the Jamia Masjid and distant ruins of Martand against a brooding Kashmiri sky

dialogue.text: In late 14th‑century Kashmir, Sultan Sikandar Shah raised mosques and schools—yet Sanskrit and Persian chronicles remember him as But‑Shikan, the breaker of temples. How did one reign carve such opposite memories?

panels.shot: slow push-in from high over Srinagar, descending toward the palace by the Jhelum

dialogue.text: Around 1389 CE, Sikandar Shah took the throne of Kashmir. The valley had already seen Shah Mir’s dynasty rise, Buddhist and Brahmin lineages fade, and rival chiefs struggle for land and temple wealth.

panels.shot: medium interior shot, slight low-angle, Sikandar in council chamber

dialogue.text: Muslim rule had taken root for half a century, yet shrines, priestly estates and older elites still held land, revenue and influence. To rule firmly, Sikandar had to decide: how far would change go?

panels.shot: wide shot of Jamia Masjid construction site in Srinagar

dialogue.text: Persian chroniclers and later historians note Sikandar’s building hand: the Jamia Masjid in Srinagar, institutions for qadis, support for schools and places of learning, hospitals and charitable endowments.

panels.shot: medium shot at Khanqah-e-Moula, devotional gathering

dialogue.text: He patronised Khanqah‑e‑Moula and Sufi institutions. In Muslim hagiographies, Sikandar appears as a pious ruler, shaping a city of mosques, shrines and disciplined law courts.

panels.shot: tight shot on Sikandar’s face in dim council chamber, half in shadow

dialogue.text: But Jonaraja, the Sanskrit court poet who lived through Sikandar’s time, tells another side: heavy jizya on non‑Muslims, bans on Brahmin teaching, exile of those who refused to bend.

panels.shot: dramatic wide shot of the valley with Martand temple ruins on a plateau

dialogue.text: Jonaraja names the shrines Sikandar’s men ruined: Martand, Vijayesvara, Cakradhara, Suresvari, Varaha, Tripuresvara. Centuries‑old stone temples, emptied and shattered in one reign.

panels.shot: medium shot at a broken temple courtyard with fallen sculptures

dialogue.text: Modern scholars debate the motives. Walter Slaje reads Jonaraja’s words as genuine religious iconoclasm. Others highlight the seizure of temple‑Brahmin wealth, crucial for shoring up Sultanate power.

panels.shot: interior shot of revenue office, Brahmin petitioners turned away

dialogue.text: Jonaraja describes jizya: a special tax for those who would not convert, and restrictions on Hindu learning. Temple teachers lost patronage; some fled. For many, religion and livelihood were tied together.

panels.shot: wide shot of a riverside scene with camps of displaced people leaving the valley

dialogue.text: The Baharistan‑i‑Shahi, a later Persian chronicle, adds harsher strokes: reports of forced conversions, punishments, and massacres of those who resisted. It praises these acts as piety, but also amplifies them.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Sikandar in prayer niche of a mosque

dialogue.text: Hagiographic traditions make him a model devout king. Historian Hakim Sameer Hamdani warns that such pious tales may exaggerate zeal, turning complex policies into simple stories of saintly iconoclasm.

panels.shot: close-up of a stone Brahma sculpture with an inscription naming Sikandar

dialogue.text: Then another piece of evidence complicates the picture: a Brahma sculpture from around 1409 CE carries a dedication naming Sikandar. Even amid temple destruction, some Hindu art and worship still found space.

panels.shot: medium shot of Sikandar hearing different advisers in a tense court

dialogue.text: Chitralekha Zutshi and others see Sikandar’s measures as both religious and political: asserting Muslim rule, weakening rival elites, redirecting wealth to mosques, offices and military obligations.

panels.shot: wide shot of Parihaspore and Bijbehara landscapes showing temple ruins and new mosques

dialogue.text: In Parihaspore, Bijbehara, Anantnag, the pattern echoed: older shrines fell, mosques and khanqahs rose, jizya marked difference. The valley’s sacred geography itself was being redrawn.

panels.shot: intimate close-up of Sikandar’s eyes looking out over the valley from a balcony

dialogue.speaker: sikandar_shah
dialogue.text: A king’s choices scar stone and memory both.

panels.shot: wide shot of court scene late in Sikandar’s reign, with younger nobles present

dialogue.text: By the time Sikandar’s reign ended around 1413 CE, Kashmir’s social balance had shifted. Many Brahmins were gone or weakened; Islamic institutions were entrenched. His successors inherited a changed valley.

panels.shot: montage-wide of manuscripts: Jonaraja’s palm-leaf, Baharistan-i-Shahi, modern books

dialogue.text: Jonaraja mourns ruined temples. Baharistan‑i‑Shahi celebrates conversions and punishments. Modern historians sift these voices, weighing bias, faith, wealth and power without erasing the hard facts.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye shot over Srinagar showing mosques, temples ruins, and bustling streets today

dialogue.text: Today, Kashmir’s landscape still carries Sikandar’s shadow: mosques and khanqahs he fostered, temple sites he broke, communities that remember exile, survival, and the slow work of coexistence.

panels.shot: slow fading close-up of Sikandar’s statue-like figure dissolving into pages of chronicles

dialogue.text: To face Sikandar Shah’s reign is to hold both mosque and broken temple in view—to speak the record fully, without hatred and without hiding—and let truth itself teach what power can do.
